articles.title: These Scams Fooled Real People—Could They Fool You Too?
articles.content:
You’d never fall for a scam, right? You know better than to send money to a mysterious prince (or princess), click a link promising you’ve won a vacation you never entered, or hand over your password to a stranger. Easy enough. Except today’s scams aren’t always that obvious. Some look, sound and feel so convincing that even the savviest among us could be fooled, and by the time you realize something’s off, the scammer may already have what they came for.
That’s why we’re sharing true stories of the sneakiest scams that tricked people—and could lure you in too if you don’t know what to look for. We’ll tell you what happened, highlight the red flags they missed and note the steps you can take to protect yourself in a similar situation.
Read on for the real-life scams that seem surprisingly legit, plus how to spot them before you become a cautionary tale for someone else.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, scams, history, cleaning, travel and fun facts all week long.
It was a sultry July day in 2025, and Christine, 86, was enjoying the air conditioning in her Philadelphia home, surrounded by photographs of her loved ones. When the phone rang, displaying a number she didn’t recognize, she answered and heard a sound no grandparent should ever be subjected to: her granddaughter’s sobs.
“What’s the matter, hon?” Christine asked. Her anguished “granddaughter,” according to NBC10, replied that she’d been injured in a car crash and was being detained by police. Before Christine could fully process the horrifying news, a new speaker joined the conversation, introducing himself as “John,” her granddaughter’s lawyer. He said he needed $10,400 to get her granddaughter out of jail. Christine said she only had $6,000 on hand in cash. That would have to do, said John. He told her he would send a car over immediately to pick it up, then kept her on the phone while another man arrived a little later for the money.
Minutes after that man left with the cash in hand, Christine’s grandson, who lives next door, showed up at her house. That’s when she learned the good news: Her granddaughter was, in fact, fine. She also learned some bad news: She had just become another victim of AI-assisted voice cloning.
Not so long ago, it was easier to spot scammers by their voices. If they sounded like impostors or recordings, you could simply hang up the phone and go about your day. Not anymore. With just a few recorded words, scammers can use AI to replicate someone’s voice and convince even family members that a loved one is in danger. The process is called voice cloning, and it’s frighteningly simple. As Christine’s granddaughter told NBC10, “It’s not hard to find something of my voice. I’m on social media.”
To protect against this, NBC recommends that you choose a security word with your family or that you ask whomever you’re talking to a question that “only a family member would know the answer to.” If that person doesn’t respond correctly, you might be talking to someone else.
If the voice on the line tells you to go buy an app or a gift card or wants payment in cryptocurrency, hang up immediately. Scammers are partial to crypto because transactions are quick, irreversible and lack the built-in protections offered by banks.
You can protect your own identity by staying quiet whenever taking suspicious or unsolicited phone calls. Don’t bother saying “Hello” (which confirms your number as active). And don’t ask to be removed from call lists, as even 10 seconds of audio may be all that the scammers need to con your family.
In an era of disinformation, stolen valor is a particularly odious scam. It’s what happens when someone lies about or misrepresents their military service to garner respect or other benefits reserved for actual heroes. Just last year, MPR News reported that a Minnesota man had been convicted of passing himself off as a wounded Marine and prisoner of war to garner over $100,000 in benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Stolen valor is not new. Among the most famous cases is one involving Jackie Stern, who wove a web of lies that began soon after he moved to Fort Lauderdale, Florida, from the New York City area in 1989. His former neighbor Alberto Lopez told the Tampa Bay Times that Stern let everyone know he’d been a Purple Heart recipient and a POW during the Korean conflict. “Out of respect for the guy, you let him talk,” said Lopez.
Stern spun his yarns and eventually greeted veterans returning home from the Gulf War in 1991 while wearing the Congressional Medal of Honor, the highest military decoration awarded by the United States. Stern claimed he’d received it for heroism. In reality, the award had been an unauthorized medal that Stern had purchased for $500 at a military memorabilia show in New Jersey, the Orlando Sentinel reported.
Stern’s lies knew no bounds. He even bragged to Broward County detectives that he’d been a New York City police detective, although he was actually a truck driver. That may have been his undoing. Detective Sgt. Daniel Ciacciarelli received a tip about a Medal of Honor stolen from the New York City area around the time Stern had arrived in Florida. Having always thought Stern was a bit of a blowhard, he checked with the Congressional Medal of Honor Society and learned there was no record of Stern receiving the honor. The detective concocted a plan. He tricked Stern into coming down to the station to pose for photographs with the medal, where he was arrested by a waiting FBI agent. It turned out that Stern, although he had served in the military, had never seen a day of combat.
For wearing an unearned military decoration and illegally modifying his official record with the Army, Stern was fined $250 and sentenced to a year on probation and 250 hours of community service at a Veterans Administration hospital. He also had to print an apology in his local newspaper for Memorial Day and—most creatively—write letters of apology to all 171 living Medal of Honor recipients at the time.
Stern admitted to the court that his goal was “personal and selfish,” reported the Orlando Sentinel, and added that he had wanted his children “to believe their father was a hero.”
According to USAMM.com, a veteran-owned retailer specializing in military medals and gear, indicators that point toward unearned medals include errors on the fraudster’s uniform, stories that don’t add up, over-the-top tales and a lack of knowledge of basic military jargon.
The National Archives cautions that lying about one’s military service is not necessarily illegal. It’s only a crime if someone lies about receiving certain medals to “obtain money, property or some other tangible benefit.” However, attempting to support these lies through forged documents, as Stern did, will likely violate separate laws.
Santiago Machado could not believe what he was hearing: a weeklong stay at the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic, for him and his extended family, for only $6,000—flights and three rooms included.
Machado, from South Florida, might have declined such telephone offers in the past, but this one sounded genuine. His friend enjoyed a Hard Rock membership, he told NBC Miami. Perhaps he had recommended Machado? The idea of a group vacation also hooked him. His mother in Cuba had never boarded an airplane before. What a nice surprise this would make!
Machado shared the news with his family and friends. Shortly after, they, too, were sending money and passport information to so-called representatives of the hotel. They were all set to go. But when some of Machado’s friends tried to change their arrival times, they found that no one at the hotel or the airline had any record of their reservations.
Outraged, Machado tried contacting the people who had sold him the package. But when he finally got through, “they were laughing,” he said.
Machado was out the $6,000. But there was also a new risk of identity theft since their personal information, passports and pictures had been shared as well. If that wasn’t enough, he now had to tell his mother and other family members in Cuba that the vacation was off. “[They all] cried when we told them … that it was all a scam and that we had lost the money,” Machado told Telemundo 51.
Machado’s first mistake was being too trusting. As the saying goes, if it looks too good to be true, chances are it is. In this case, looking online reveals that three rooms for three days at the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Punta Cana alone—without airfare—could run close to $6,000. Aside from an oddly cheap price, any typos or peculiar word choices in your exchanges with the “owners” should also make you think twice. Legit operations tend to know how to spell.
Before you put down a deposit, Navy Federal Credit Union suggests you make sure the hotel or vacation rental actually exists. You can do that by looking it up using Google Maps Street View and checking whether the property matches the picture in the listing, and by calling the front desk to verify the information if it’s a resort or hotel.
And never pay for a vacation rental by wire transfer, prepaid card, gift cards or apps like Venmo, as these payment methods aren’t easily reversible. Instead, Better Business Bureau spokesperson Cinthya Lavin told NBC Miami, pay with a credit card, which offers some protections.
Jeanette Voss, a retiree in Vermont, had her 2021 Memorial Day Weekend all planned out. And part of it would be spent watching a movie on her laptop. However, halfway into the film, a “screaming noise” blared from her computer, and then a pop-up filled the screen. The message was clear enough, she told AARP: “Call Microsoft. Call Microsoft.”
Voss picked up her phone and called the number on the screen, assuming she’d be connected to a Microsoft specialist. After getting the noise to stop, the “specialist” passed Voss on to more specialists, one supposedly from her financial institution. Yet another came on and told her, “We can see where you made a gambling bet of $213,000.”
“I most certainly did not,” she replied. She then heard those words that you never want to hear in the same sentence: hackers and Social Security number. Voss’s movie night was ruined.
The man explained they would need to transfer all her assets into a “secure digital wallet” for safekeeping, she told Seven Days, a Vermont newspaper. In the meantime, the man warned, “trust no one.” Jeanette agreed, and over the next six months she spoke repeatedly to two men, using a prepaid cellphone because hers was “compromised.”
All of Voss’s assets, including retirement savings and stocks that she had carefully managed for years, were moved with her assistance into online accounts and cryptocurrency wallets that totaled nearly $950,000. And then the conversations ended and the money was gone.The loss was life-changing, forcing Voss to completely alter her spending habits. All she had to live on were her monthly Social Security checks, which were barely enough to make ends meet. She cut back on groceries, unplugged devices when she wasn’t using them and had to miss a funeral because of travel costs. She became isolated, spending her days just with the birds and squirrels outside her door. Her life, she told Seven Days, was one of “unrelenting stress.”
But then, a miracle. Four and a half years later, in December 2025, Voss found out that Secret Service agents had traced her funds to a cryptocurrency account associated with a man involved in an international scam ring, Vermont Public Radio reported: “After seizing the crypto wallet, government officials sold the tokens in order to compensate Voss.” It was a rare victory for the good guys against the dark web. To celebrate, Voss bought groceries for herself, and for the birds and squirrels that “kept me sane.”
The fake alert that so alarmed Voss was likely accidentally downloaded days or even weeks earlier when she clicked on an ad in, say, Facebook, Doug Shadel, a fraud expert, told Seven Days. When “this pop-up occurs with a phone number to call and sirens going off, you call the number because you’re panicked,” he explained. If this should happen to you, Microsoft says to immediately close your browser. If it won’t close, restart your computer.
Still unnerved? Keep in mind that tech companies like Microsoft usually direct users to official websites and support pages, never to phone numbers provided in pop-up windows. Also, no major computer company will ever request that you pay them via cryptocurrency or gift cards.
And always remember: While there are some wonderful things about the internet (funny beagle videos, obviously!), there are also questionable characters lurking about waiting for you to inadvertently hit the wrong link. So be skeptical if someone asks for personal information or offers you a deal that’s too good to be true. It probably is.

articles.title: This Fall Comfort Food Actually Tastes Better the Next Day—Here’s What Should Be in Your Leftover Stash
articles.content:
With daylight saving now in the rearview mirror, it’s tough to drum up the energy to make dinner every night when it’s fully dark out before 5 p.m. At this time of year, I often lean on recipes that will feed my family for two or three nights as opposed to just one, and as it turns out, one of my favorite fall comfort foods actually tastes better on Day 2 and beyond.
I swear, it’s not just my imagination—or my brain doing overtime to make me feel better about my lack of motivation. In fact, I got corroboration from Helen Rennie, the owner of Helen’s Kitchen Cooking School and the author of the forthcoming cookbook The Science of Dinner, who said there’s a definite culinary benefit to letting that soup sit. Translation: Make a big batch, eat it for days and don’t feel one bit guilty about it.
Read on to find out why she says this dinnertime staple is best eaten after it spends some time in the fridge.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food news, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Soup! There are a few reasons why this happens, but a big part of it involves the role of smell and how you experience taste because of it. Research shows that between 75% and 95% of what we think of as taste actually comes from our sense of smell. Um, OK, but what does this have to do with leftover soup? “Sometimes it’s not the soup that’s different the next day but how your brain registers the smell,” Rennie says.
Let’s say you’re in the kitchen while your soup is simmering away, and your nose is picking up on the delicious aromas the entire time. “The problem is that you get acclimated to them,” Rennie explains. “Our brains are built to notice the difference in smell, not just the presence of smell. When you reheat the soup the next day, your sense of smell is reset, and all the aromas in your soup are new and exciting to your nose and brain again.” The result, in many cases, is that the flavors taste bigger and bolder than they did the first time.
But that’s not all: The ingredients you put into the soup interact with one another and evolve over time. When you make something savory (like most soups), the two tastes that most impact the flavor are salt and acidity. “If your soup will be pureed, the salt will be evenly distributed,” Rennie says. “But if your soup is chunky, the salt will need time to absorb into your ingredients. As the soup rests, salt and acid can redistribute between the broth and the solid ingredients, changing how each component tastes.”
In other words, letting your soup spend a night in the fridge will allow the flavors to mix and mingle in a way that makes them taste that much better the next day.
As noted above, you’re going to see the most noticeable improvement in taste in chunky soups and stews that you refrigerate overnight. For pureed soups, “a long resting period will not result in any improvement in taste,” Rennie says, since the original blending process evenly distributes all the ingredients and seasonings. That doesn’t mean a bisque will taste bad as leftovers; it just won’t be obviously better.
If your soup contains rice, noodles, delicate greens or fresh herbs, consider storing those items separately from your leftover soup and adding them during reheating. Rennie notes that rice and noodles can get mushy if they’re left in the broth, while greens and herbs can lose their bright color and fresh aromas during storage—all of which can make for a lesser soup-eating experience the next day.
The same is true of fish. “If you are making a fish soup, you can make stock days in advance, but don’t add the fish fillets to the soup until right before serving,” Rennie adds. “Rewarming soup with fish can result in overcooking.”
“Most soups keep well in the fridge for up to five days,” says Rennie. That’s on the long end in terms of how long most leftovers last, which is another bonus. There’s no peak time to reheat and serve soup to maximize the flavor, but you may need to adjust the salt or acidity (with a splash of lemon juice or vinegar) as you get to days three, four or five.
The exceptions to this rule, Rennie says, are fish soups, which keep for only two days in the fridge, and cold soups that contain raw ingredients, which keep for just one. That said, most soups last in the freezer for two to three months, Rennie notes.
You may know that pasta and rice are healthier as leftovers, thanks to the development of something called resistant starch during the cooling process. Resistant starch contributes to a healthier gut microbiome, better blood-sugar control, lower cholesterol and higher feelings of satiety. While pasta and rice are the biggies, beans, lentils and potatoes also develop resistant starch during cooling, so if your soup contains any of these ingredients you are going to reap these benefits.
Otherwise, soup isn’t going to be any healthier (or unhealthier, for that matter) on subsequent days than it was on the first.
There’s nothing dangerous about reheating and eating leftover soup—as long as you’re cooling and storing it safely. You can’t finish making a batch and immediately put that hot pot of soup in the fridge, Rennie says, because it can warm your entire fridge to a temperature that puts all of your food in the danger zone for bacterial growth. (That’s between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit, by the way.) But at the same time, you can’t leave the soup out for hours and hours until it’s cool enough to put in the fridge, since that would likely mean it’s spending quite a bit of time in that dangerous temperature range.
The sweet spot, according to Rennie, is cooling your soup at room temperature for two to four hours after you finish cooking it before transferring it to the fridge. “If you want to speed up this process, set the pot into a clean sink filled with ice water and stir the soup frequently,” she suggests.
If you can’t put your whole pot of soup in the fridge, here’s what to do.

Soup! There are a few reasons why this happens, but a big part of it involves the role of smell and how you experience taste because of it. Research shows that between 75% and 95% of what we think of as taste actually comes from our sense of smell. Um, OK, but what does this have to do with leftover soup? “Sometimes it’s not the soup that’s different the next day but how your brain registers the smell,” Rennie says.

Let’s say you’re in the kitchen while your soup is simmering away, and your nose is picking up on the delicious aromas the entire time. “The problem is that you get acclimated to them,” Rennie explains. “Our brains are built to notice the difference in smell, not just the presence of smell. When you reheat the soup the next day, your sense of smell is reset, and all the aromas in your soup are new and exciting to your nose and brain again.” The result, in many cases, is that the flavors taste bigger and bolder than they did the first time.

But that’s not all: The ingredients you put into the soup interact with one another and evolve over time. When you make something savory (like most soups), the two tastes that most impact the flavor are salt and acidity. “If your soup will be pureed, the salt will be evenly distributed,” Rennie says. “But if your soup is chunky, the salt will need time to absorb into your ingredients. As the soup rests, salt and acid can redistribute between the broth and the solid ingredients, changing how each component tastes.”

In other words, letting your soup spend a night in the fridge will allow the flavors to mix and mingle in a way that makes them taste that much better the next day.

What soups does this work best with?

As noted above, you’re going to see the most noticeable improvement in taste in chunky soups and stews that you refrigerate overnight. For pureed soups, “a long resting period will not result in any improvement in taste,” Rennie says, since the original blending process evenly distributes all the ingredients and seasonings. That doesn’t mean a bisque will taste bad as leftovers; it just won’t be obviously better.

If your soup contains rice, noodles, delicate greens or fresh herbs, consider storing those items separately from your leftover soup and adding them during reheating. Rennie notes that rice and noodles can get mushy if they’re left in the broth, while greens and herbs can lose their bright color and fresh aromas during storage—all of which can make for a lesser soup-eating experience the next day.

The same is true of fish. “If you are making a fish soup, you can make stock days in advance, but don’t add the fish fillets to the soup until right before serving,” Rennie adds. “Rewarming soup with fish can result in overcooking.”

How long can you eat leftover soup?

“Most soups keep well in the fridge for up to five days,” says Rennie. That’s on the long end in terms of how long most leftovers last, which is another bonus. There’s no peak time to reheat and serve soup to maximize the flavor, but you may need to adjust the salt or acidity (with a splash of lemon juice or vinegar) as you get to days three, four or five.

The exceptions to this rule, Rennie says, are fish soups, which keep for only two days in the fridge, and cold soups that contain raw ingredients, which keep for just one. That said, most soups last in the freezer for two to three months, Rennie notes.

Is leftover soup healthier than the fresh-off-the-stove batch?

You may know that pasta and rice are healthier as leftovers, thanks to the development of something called resistant starch during the cooling process. Resistant starch contributes to a healthier gut microbiome, better blood-sugar control, lower cholesterol and higher feelings of satiety. While pasta and rice are the biggies, beans, lentils and potatoes also develop resistant starch during cooling, so if your soup contains any of these ingredients you are going to reap these benefits.

Otherwise, soup isn’t going to be any healthier (or unhealthier, for that matter) on subsequent days than it was on the first.

Are there any potential dangers to eating leftover soup?

There’s nothing dangerous about reheating and eating leftover soup—as long as you’re cooling and storing it safely. You can’t finish making a batch and immediately put that hot pot of soup in the fridge, Rennie says, because it can warm your entire fridge to a temperature that puts all of your food in the danger zone for bacterial growth. (That’s between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit, by the way.) But at the same time, you can’t leave the soup out for hours and hours until it’s cool enough to put in the fridge, since that would likely mean it’s spending quite a bit of time in that dangerous temperature range.

The sweet spot, according to Rennie, is cooling your soup at room temperature for two to four hours after you finish cooking it before transferring it to the fridge. “If you want to speed up this process, set the pot into a clean sink filled with ice water and stir the soup frequently,” she suggests.

What’s the best way to store soup?

If you can’t put your whole pot of soup in the fridge, here’s what to do.

  • Divide it up. Store the soup in smaller containers that make sense for your family. “A pint will typically serve one, a quart will serve two, and two quarts will serve four people,” Rennie says. “Portioning soup into containers will help it cool faster and will free up space in your fridge after every meal of soup.”
  • Don’t cover containers right away. After you split the soup into containers, place them in the fridge uncovered until the soup is cold. “This will help cool the soup faster and prevent moisture from condensing on the lid,” Rennie explains.
  • Keep mushy and delicate ingredients separate. I mentioned this earlier, but if you’re making a soup with noodles, rice, fresh greens or fresh herbs and you plan to eat the leftovers for a few days, consider cooking the noodles or rice separately and adding them to the soup by the serving to avoid mushiness. Likewise, add fresh greens and herbs during reheating so they don’t lose their flavors.
  • Don’t freeze potatoes. Chunks of potatoes get spongy in the freezer, so soups like chowders that contain them are best kept in the fridge. “Pureed potato soups can become grainy after freezing and might need re-blending,” Rennie adds.

Sources:

articles.title: Here’s How to Make a Time Capsule That’ll Last Your Family for Generations
articles.content:
It’s hard to forget the day your elementary school class buried a time capsule—the excitement of knowing that someday future students and teachers, or maybe even you and your classmates at your 30-year reunion, would get a glimpse of what your life was like. Maybe you tucked in a fact sheet listing your favorite foods, video games, school subjects and closest friends, or a letter to your future self predicting flying cars. Or maybe you and your best friend stuffed a coffee can with friendship bracelets, the names of your crushes and a mixtape of your favorite songs.
These days, it may seem as though a time capsule wouldn’t be worth making when a quick online search can turn up old yearbook photos, newspaper archives and videos of just about anything you ever played with or listened to. But nothing compares to holding the real thing: the soft crease of a handwritten letter, the rough, snaggly hair of a vintage Barbie doll, the crackling of a well-worn single on a record player. Objects that were actually there at the time carry a look and feel no screen can match, and that’s exactly what a time capsule preserves.
So if you’re wondering how to make a time capsule as a grown-up, here’s the good news: It’s not only easy—it’s also even more meaningful the second time around, especially when you do it with your family. That’s because it’s a literal snapshot of who you are right now: the jokes everyone repeats at dinner, what the kids want to be when they grow up, what a gallon of milk costs, and the way Grandma signs her name.
